articles.body:
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

articles.body:
China

At a neon-lit electronics market in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, buyers from Africa to Bangladesh are snapping up dozens of used smartphones.

The number is mind-boggling. As the world's largest smartphone producer, China discards over 400 million devices annually.

"From all China, the broken mobile phones come here," said Pakistani businessman Akhtar Muhammad as he browsed the stacks of devices.

"We will buy the new LCDs, send the broken phones to our countries, also buy LCDs from here take them to Pakistan where we will fix them," he said.

Chip shortages and rising prices are making new devices harder to afford and in emerging markets in Africa and South Asia the demand for used models is soaring.

Counterpoint Research says the global secondary smartphone market grew 13 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 150 million units.

Mama, a young Nigerian buyer, said he had bought around 40 used phones in one day in Shenzhen.

"They are more expensive in Africa because we don't have big suppliers or markets like this one," he said. "If I buy and send them to my country, I get profit."

But near the market in Shenzhen, a new and more formalised alternative is taking root. PaiJiTang Mall is a self-service second-hand marketplace run by Chinese recycling company ATRenew.

Inside, rows of over 20,000 used phones are on display. Buyers scan QR codes for instant inspection reports and pricing, test the units and purchase in bulk.

The shop draws up to 1,000 visitors daily, with international traders making up about a third, said store manager Zhang Xiaoming.

Algerian shopkeeper, Abdul Rahim, says he flies to China up to three times a month to stock his phone and accessory store, capitalising on a price gap of $110 to $132 per device.

"It's very easy for Algerians to get the visa to China. You put in your papers and in two or three days you have the visa in your passport," he said.

At ATRenew's massive processing hub in Dongguan, north of Shenzhen, roughly 30,000 second-hand gadgets arrive daily and are inspected and packed by over 300 technicians.

Its quality control manager, Li Cankang, says its daily outbound shipments are at a similar level.

Apple devices account for 70 to 80 per cent of sales, with the rest split among Chinese brands.

Counterpoint says while older models like the iPhone 11, 12, and 13 are losing ground to cheap Androids in China, they retain strong brand power overseas, where they find a second life.

articles.body:
This comes amid efforts by Indonesia to strengthen enforcement, bolster market integrity and protect investors.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) on Saturday (Nov 21) announced sanctions in 10 capital market violation cases, amid efforts to strengthen enforcement, bolster market integrity and protect investors.

OJK ordered the return of 23.77 billion rupiah (US$1.3 million) in illicit gains from three stock manipulation cases, involving shares of PT Grand House Mulia, PT Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur and PT Suryamas Dutamakmur.

In the Grand House Mulia case, OJK also ordered the closure of 15 securities accounts linked to the trading activity between March and July 2023.

The agency also imposed a total of 3.71 billion rupiah in administrative fines on seven listed companies for disclosure failures, material and affiliated-party transaction breaches, financial reporting violations and non-compliance with share transfer obligations.

OJK also barred multiple individuals involved in the manipulation cases from participating in Indonesia's capital markets, derivatives and carbon exchange sectors for periods ranging from three to 10 years.

OJK previously sanctioned three listed firms as part of Indonesia's market reforms following concerns raised by global index providers over the transparency and investability of Indonesia's capital markets.

articles.title: Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once
articles.summary: Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher, as senior military commanders touted the Islamic Republic's capabilities in defiant messages to the United States. "A launcher capable of firing two liquid-propellant missiles simultaneously was unveiled for the first time," Iranian state television reported on Saturday. State television broadcast footage of Ahmad Vahidi, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Majid Mousavi, head of the IRGC's Aerospace Force, touring an underground missile base. The two commanders were shown riding on top of a vehicle through long tunnels lined with missiles, launchers and other military equipment. "The damage suffered by our enemy is only the beginning. During the US-Israeli war on Iran, strikes targeted the country's missile capabilities and hit its nuclear sites for a second time, though the extent of the damage remains unclear. Una nave russa ormeggiata nel porto di Bengasi è stata colpita in quello che si sospetta essere stato un attacco condotto con droni e l'esplosione non ha provocato vittime. Lo scrive Anadolu citando le autorità della Libia orientale.

"Le indagini preliminari indicano che l'esplosione è avvenuta a bordo di una nave russa ormeggiata nel porto", ha detto in un comunicato l'amministrazione dell'est del Paese del comandante Khalifa Haftar. "Si sospetta che la nave sia stata colpita da droni. L'imbarcazione era in viaggio verso la Russia e aveva effettuato una sosta per il rifornimento di carburante e di provviste".

L'azione è "un attacco a lungo raggio condotto dal Servizio di sicurezza dell'Ucraina (Sbu)": lo riporta su X Barak Ravid, giornalista di Axios e Channel 12 News, citando "una fonte a conoscenza" dell'accaduto.

La nave russa colpita era la corvetta della marina militare russa Merkury, classe Steregushchiy, per un valore di circa 150 milioni di sterline. Lo riporta Sky News citando Naval News secondo cui l'imbarcazione si trovava nella base navale di Bengasi già da diversi giorni prima dell'attacco. Sempre secondo Naval News la nave è stata "quasi certamente distrutta".

Il governo della Libia orientale guidato da Osama Hammad ha denunciato come una grave violazione della sovranità nazionale l'esplosione avvenuta all'alba di oggi nella base navale di Bengasi, che secondo i risultati preliminari delle indagini si sarebbe verificata a bordo di una nave russa ormeggiata nel porto. "L'attacco contro una nave all'interno di un porto libico costituisce una grave aggressione alla sovranità nazionale e una flagrante violazione della sicurezza dei porti e della navigazione marittima", sottolinea il comunicato, precisando che l'episodio "non può essere considerato un semplice incidente né qualcosa su cui si possa soprassedere".

A nuoto per tre giorni attraverso le acque di Hormuz, avanzando a bracciate lungo 15 chilometri per trasmettere un messaggio di pace forte e chiaro: "Basta combattimenti. Aprite lo Stretto. Ripulitelo dall'inquinamento". E' la missione in cui si è lanciato Lewis Pugh, 56enne britannico specializzato in nuoto di resistenza, e conclusa nella giornata di sabato, come riportato dal Guardian e altri media internazionali.

Già protagonista di altre lunghe traversate volte a sensibilizzare su cause politiche sociali (ad esempio al Polo Nord) Pugh, che è anche riconosciuto come ambasciatore degli Oceani dalle Nazioni Unite, ha scelto per la prima volta di nuotare in una zona di conflitto. Perché, come lui stesso ha spiegato in un post su Instagram, la situazione dell'area di Hormuz è ora emblema di due delle questioni che più preoccupano il pianeta: i conflitti bellici e la crisi climatica, che in quel tratto di mare si incrociano.

"La guerra provoca immense sofferenze umane. Si perdono vite, famiglie vengono distrutte e case rase al suolo. Ma c'è un'altra vittima a cui viene dedicata fin troppo poca attenzione: la natura stessa", afferma Pugh. Questo stretto che separa le coste dell'Oman e dell'Iran è infatti "una delle grandi meraviglie del mondo", con le sue "montagne imponenti che si innalzano su fiordi spettacolari". Ma ora "questo luogo straordinario si trova nel mezzo di un conflitto", con "petroliere, navi metaniere e altre imbarcazioni commerciali che vengono attaccate". Una crisi le cui "conseguenze ambientali dureranno per decenni".

Pugh, che ha nuotato in un braccio di mare compreso tra l'isola di Musandam e Capo Hormuz, lungo il lato omanita dello Stretto, ha detto di esser stato diretto testimone di episodi che dimostrano cosa sta accadendo lì. "Appena 30 minuti dopo aver iniziato a nuotare, una petroliera è stata colpita a pochi chilometri di distanza. Le esplosioni hanno fatto tremare il mare intorno a me. Nei giorni successivi, ho assistito ad altri attacchi contro il traffico marittimo commerciale e ho visto alcune imbarcazioni avvolte dalle fiamme", ha raccontato. Ora chiede aiuto per "diffondere il messaggio" contro la guerra e contro l'inquinamento che provoca.

articles.body:
There was no immediate reaction from Russia, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

A suspected sea drone attack has hit a Russian vessel at a naval base in eastern Libya, causing an explosion and a brief fire, according to the North African country’s eastern-based government.

The Reuters news agency reported that an unidentified number of people were injured in the attack at the Benghazi naval base on the Mediterranean Sea on Sunday. The nationalities of the casualties were not immediately known.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s Benghazi-based administration, the eastern government said. It gave no details about the vessel or its cargo.

The administration said it had launched a joint investigation with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it”.

The government said the fire had been brought under control and the site secured, while it condemned the suspected strike as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety.

‘Exporting international conflicts’

“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said, adding that Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea.

On Saturday, a drone struck a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland’s border guard attributed the strike to Ukraine.

A Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast in March after an attack that Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine, while last December, Ukraine said it had used aerial drones to strike a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011.

A United Nations-recognised government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

articles.body:
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

An inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.

In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.

Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”

Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.

Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Reuters contributed to this report

Fidan also described an ongoing "hidden struggle" in the United States between forces that put "Israel first" and those that put "America first". He said US policy in the Middle East had for decades often served Israeli interests more than American ones, and that Netanyahu's policies had harmed Trump. "Trump, who boasted of being a man who makes peace, seemed to have become a president who enters wars instead of achieving peace, and who fights on behalf of Israel," Fidan said. He added that a growing current in the US was rejecting military intervention, and that public hostility towards Israel was rising. Fidan also defended Turkey's role in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, which commits each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all three. He said Ankara was giving Riyadh the defence support it needed, but accused critics in Turkey of exaggerating the pact. He dismissed warnings in Turkey that soldiers would die in Yemen's desert, saying that unlike a century ago, when Yemen was Ottoman territory, it was now an independent state. He also noted that Turkey had sent troops to Afghanistan as part of Nato without facing similar criticism. "Why was there no problem when it concerned Nato, while there is a problem when it concerns a regional defence alliance in an Islamic region?" he said. articles.body:
Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

“Relying on fuel imports during an era of benign international relations and dependable strategic partners was a passable strategy. But in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, it is no longer tenable,” the report, released on Sunday, warned.

“Australia should expect the coming decades to be less stable than the past one. This means bracing, and preparing, for more oil shocks.”

Australia imports 97% of its liquid fuel. Grattan’s fuel plan report, Fuelling the Future, warns this “leaves us dangerously exposed to supply disruptions and price hikes”.

It argues that the US-Israel war in Iran has driven up inflation and cost Australians nearly $18bn, and the federal government directly at least $3bn, creating an opportunity the government “should seize” to boost fuel security.

Very little liquid fuel is produced or refined in Australia, with only two domestic oil refineries. But rather than boosting that number, Grattan says Australia should lower its reliance on imported fuels and fossil fuels generally by shifting towards EVs, including an ambitious target of 650,000 electric trucks nationwide by 2050.

That alone would cut Australia’s diesel use by 5bn litres a year, Grattan forecast. The report also calls for the fuel tax credit program – which costs Australia billions each year – to be capped at $35m per corporate group annually.

The biggest user of that program – which refunds taxes on fuel for machinery and heavy vehicles travelling on private, rather than public, roads – is the mining sector. The fuel tax credit scheme has become a political hot-button issue, with big business campaigning for it to be preserved amid calls for it to be reined in.

Tania Constable, CEO of the Minerals Council of Australia, rejected the Grattan proposal.

“Australia does need stronger fuel security, but making diesel more expensive for regional industries won’t create a single extra litre of fuel, build a refinery or improve supply-chain resilience. Instead, it would increase costs for miners, farmers, freight operators and regional businesses, with those costs ultimately flowing through to Australian households,” she said.

“If the goal is greater energy security, then Australia should be focused on increasing domestic production, expanding refining capacity and building more resilient supply chains – not making essential fuel more expensive.”

But the Grattan report says capping the scheme would save the government $3bn annually, and hasten the electrification of the mining sector – which it said would help the mining sector in the long run.

The report also recommends the government invest $1.1bn in a national network of chargers for EVs, as well as provide $2.4bn in vouchers for trucking firms to buy electric trucks. It calls for federal vehicle standards to be boosted to incentivise cleaner cars, as well as a restructuring of EV subsidies “to target people least able to afford them”.

Labor is widely expected to restrict current EV subsidies in next month’s mid-year economic update, as the government searches for budget savings.

In other areas of fuel use, Grattan notes Australia produces no “clean” jet fuel, and recommends the government direct $6bn to the first generation of so-called “clean refineries” to make that fuel.

Grattan says these refineries could provide nearly 10bn litres of clean jet fuel per year by 2050, but notes that it could cost $100bn to build them all, and that importing clean jet fuel would be cheaper.

But it argues that $6bn – the savings generated from just two years of capping the fuel tax credits to mining companies – would cover a quarter of the cost of the first five refineries, kickstarting the sector and providing fuel security in future supply shocks.

“Historically, making fuel meant making fossil fuels. But in an age of electrification and clean fuels, Australia now has more options,” the report said.

articles.title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war

articles.body:
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

articles.title: Ukraine: Up to seven feared trapped beneath rubble near Kyiv after Russian attack
articles.summary: A Russian strike partially destroyed an apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, on Sunday. Nine people, including a child, were evacuated as rescuers searched the rubble for up to seven others feared trapped.
articles.preview: Emergency workers rushed to the scene in Dymer, near Kyiv, where a Russian drone strike had destroyed a section of a five-storey residential building from the first to the fifth floor. Footage released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service showed rescuers using an extended fire ladder and an aerial platform to help residents escape from the damaged structure, while other teams searched through piles of debris for possible survivors. According to Ukrainian authorities, nine residents, including one child, had been evacuated.
articles.body: Emergency workers rushed to the scene in Dymer, near Kyiv, where a Russian drone strike had destroyed a section of a five-storey residential building from the first to the fifth floor. Footage released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service showed rescuers using an extended fire ladder and an aerial platform to help residents escape from the damaged structure, while other teams searched through piles of debris for possible survivors. According to Ukrainian authorities, nine residents, including one child, had been evacuated. The State Emergency Service initially said that up to seven people could be trapped beneath the rubble. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said that 14 people were unaccounted for. The attack was part of a wider wave of Russian drone strikes reported across Ukraine overnight. Ukraine’s Air Force said 186 attack drones were launched, of which 161 were shot down. In Kharkiv, a strike drone hit the Kyivskyi district and started a fire. In Chernihiv, a Russian strike set a wood-processing plant ablaze, while in Zaporizhzhia three people, including two children, were injured in an evening attack. The extent of the destruction in Dymer raised fears for residents who might still be beneath the collapsed sections of the building. Rescue workers remained focused on removing debris and reaching potentially trapped people, with no confirmed outcome for those still missing at the time of the initial reports. The latest strikes once again exposed the dangers faced by civilians in residential areas as Russian aerial attacks continue across Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine: Dashcam captures massive explosion on Lviv street
articles.summary: A dashcam captured the moment a Russian projectile struck a building directly ahead of a car in Lviv, forcing the driver to reverse. The attack killed two people and injured at least 10 others.
articles.preview: The footage, recorded by a driver travelling through Lviv on Friday 20 November, shows the moment a projectile struck a building directly ahead of the vehicle. The impact sent debris across the road and forced the driver to reverse sharply before driving away. Two people were killed and at least 10 others injured in Lviv’s Zaliznychnyi district as a large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage tore across the western Ukrainian city and its surrounding region, igniting fires in residential blocks and garages.
articles.body: The footage, recorded by a driver travelling through Lviv on Friday 20 November, shows the moment a projectile struck a building directly ahead of the vehicle. The impact sent debris across the road and forced the driver to reverse sharply before driving away. Two people were killed and at least 10 others injured in Lviv’s Zaliznychnyi district as a large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage tore across the western Ukrainian city and its surrounding region, igniting fires in residential blocks and garages. According to Ukrainian authorities, the bombardment left a trail of destruction spanning homes, vehicles, a dormitory, a warehouse and critical energy infrastructure, while also damaging a ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station. The fallout extended beyond the city limits into the nearby Zolochiv district, where debris from a downed Russian drone damaged three houses and a vehicle, leaving one further person injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, in the wider assault. The strikes also affected Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, underscoring the scale of the bombardment and the continuing threat to civilians and essential infrastructure.

articles.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.
articles.preview: November 21, 2026 The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea. Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.
articles.body:
November 21, 2026

The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

What do we know?

Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

What are the other latest developments in the war in Ukraine?

Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia also struck a cargo vessel near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military.

Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.

One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."

After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.preview: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz: Athlete swims through war zone to expose war's environmental toll

articles.preview: Wearing nothing but swimming trunks, goggles and a UN-branded cap, 56-year-old ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh entered the waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, where he found himself swimming within sight of burning ships and towering plumes of smoke. Just 20 minutes into his first swim, two explosions rocked the area and an oil tanker caught fire around four kilometres away, forcing him to abandon the attempt temporarily. The following day, he witnessed another vessel engulfed in flames as he continued his swim through the strategic waterway. A United Nations Patron of the Oceans, Pugh warned that pollution from damaged tankers could devastate coral reefs, mangroves and coastal ecosystems for decades. Yet sightings of dolphins, turtles and ospreys reminded him of the extraordinary wildlife at risk. Having previously swum in the Arctic, Antarctic and Red Sea to raise awareness of ocean conservation, he delivered a stark appeal: “We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up this mess.”

articles.title: Dai falsi allarmi bomba agli attacchi informatici, siamo davvero al centro di una guerra ibrida?
articles.summary: Per comprendere gli eventi, occorre inserirli in un contesto più ampio e analizzare quanto siano una minaccia concreta per l’Italia e l’Europa
articles.preview: Nelle scorse settimane, una serie di episodi che hanno interessato diversi Paesi europei, tra cui l’Italia, ha riportato al centro del dibattito pubblico il tema della “guerra ibrida”. Dagli attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei supermercati e delle banche del sangue, agli allarmi bomba che hanno bloccato aeroporti e scuole italiane ed europee.
articles.body:
Nelle scorse settimane, una serie di episodi che hanno interessato diversi Paesi europei, tra cui l’Italia, ha riportato al centro del dibattito pubblico il tema della “guerra ibrida”. Dagli attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei supermercati e delle banche del sangue, agli allarmi bomba che hanno bloccato aeroporti e scuole italiane ed europee.

Si tratta di un’espressione utilizzata sempre più spesso per descrivere forme di conflitto che si sviluppano anche al di fuori dei tradizionali scenari militari, ma che nelle ultime settimane è stata spesso impiegata in modo generico, talvolta per indicare episodi di cui non è ancora chiara la matrice. Sui social network e sulle testate giornalistiche sono circolate diverse ipotesi sui possibili responsabili dei vari attacchi e minacce, con riferimenti ad ambienti filorussi e iraniani. Nel frattempo, in Italia, le email con falsi allarmi bomba inviate a migliaia di istituti scolastici hanno aperto un dibattito sulle modalità di gestione delle minacce. Da una parte, sui social e nel dibattito pubblico, sono emerse critiche nei confronti degli istituti che hanno disposto l’evacuazione degli edifici, con l’accusa di aver contribuito ad alimentare il panico sulla base di una minaccia che era “palesemente” infondata. Dall’altra, dirigenti scolastici hanno ricordato la responsabilità di garantire la sicurezza di studenti e personale, in un contesto in cui anche una minaccia apparentemente poco credibile non può essere semplicemente ignorata.

Per comprendere la portata di questi episodi e capire quanto siano fondate le preoccupazioni emerse nelle ultime settimane, è necessario ricostruire anzitutto che cosa è successo, distinguendo i fatti accertati dalle ipotesi sui possibili responsabili. Ma anche provare a collocare questi eventi in un contesto più ampio e capire cioè se e in che modo si inseriscano nelle dinamiche della guerra ibrida, quali obiettivi possano perseguire e quanto rappresentino una minaccia concreta per l’Italia e, più in generale, per l’Europa.

Falsi allarmi bomba e attacchi hacker agli impianti di refrigerazione

Il primo episodio che ha catturato l’attenzione di media e opinione pubblica si è verificato in Francia tra l’11 e il 12 ottobre 2026, quando un attacco informatico ha colpito centinaia di supermercati e i loro sistemi di refrigerazione, provocando lo spreco di tonnellate di alimenti e danni per milioni di euro.

Il 19 ottobre falsi allarmi bomba hanno raggiunto centinaia di scuole in Irlanda del Nord, Scozia, Ungheria e Serbia, mentre pochi giorni dopo, il 2 novembre, una nuova ondata ha coinvolto 280 istituti italiani, destinatari di email che annunciavano la presenza di ordigni che in realtà non sono stati mai ritrovati. Nella stessa giornata, attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione hanno interessato supermercati in diversi Paesi europei, tra cui l’Italia, mentre due gruppi di hacker filorussi, NoName057(16) e Z-Pentest, ne rivendicavano la responsabilità. Il 4 novembre è toccato ad alcuni impianti frigoriferi dell’Istituto francese del sangue, ente pubblico ufficiale responsabile della gestione delle donazioni di sangue e della medicina trasfusionale in tutta la Francia, senza che le donazioni conservate subissero danni.

Nei giorni successivi, le minacce si sono spostate anche sul trasporto aereo. Tra il 3 e il 5 novembre, infatti, segnalazioni di esplosivi a bordo hanno coinvolto decine di voli europei, alcuni diretti in Italia o in partenza dal nostro Paese, costringendo a dirottamenti e all’attivazione dei protocolli di sicurezza. Anche in questi casi non è stato trovato alcun ordigno.

L’11 novembre circa 6 mila scuole italiane hanno ricevuto nuove email con falsi allarmi bomba, provocando l’evacuazione di centinaia di istituti. «Abbiamo piazzato una bomba nel motore dell’auto del vostro primo ministro», si legge nella mail, firmata da un mittente che si presentava come “Mikhail Andropov”, leader del “Vilayat di Misoginistan”, pseudonimo che era comparso anche in altri falsi allarmi bomba nei giorni precedenti. La vicenda ha spinto il governo a riunire i vertici dell’intelligence e della cybersicurezza e a confrontarsi con le opposizioni. Il 16 novembre si è verificata un’ulteriore ondata di minacce, firmate ancora una volta “Mikhail Andropov”. Questa volta, però, le scuole non sono state evacuate in modo automatico e massivo. In base alle nuove indicazioni del Viminale, infatti, la sola ricezione di un’email non è sufficiente a disporre lo sgombero, che spetta al Prefetto in presenza di ulteriori elementi indicativi di un pericolo concreto.

Un quadro che si è costruito nel tempo

I recenti episodi italiani ed europei hanno acceso i riflettori su un fenomeno che, in realtà, ha una storia ben lunga e non nasce con le ultime settimane di allarmi, minacce ed effettivi attacchi.

Il tema della sicurezza delle tecnologie dell’informazione e della comunicazione è al centro del confronto internazionale da almeno vent’anni. Nel 2015, infatti le Nazioni Unite hanno concordato undici regole di comportamento per un uso responsabile delle tecnologie digitali, riconoscendo anche che il diritto internazionale si applica a questo ambito. Oggi esiste anche un meccanismo permanente di dialogo, il Global Mechanism, cioè un foro permanente dedicato alla sicurezza informatica e alla governance dello spazio cibernetico. Sul piano europeo, invece, il quadro sulle minacce ibride risale al 2016, al quale sono seguiti altri strumenti negli anni successivi, fino a un protocollo per la risposta coordinata del 2023.

Nel corso di un’audizione alla Commissione Affari esteri e difesa del Senato, il 13 ottobre 2026, Andrea Quacivi, direttore generale dell’Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale, ha spiegato che nei primi nove mesi del 2026 l’agenzia ha rilevato «3.271 eventi cyber, a fronte dei 2.729 registrati nell’intero 2025» aggiungendo che di questi, 1.922 sono stati classificati come incidenti con impatto confermato, un dato in aumento rispetto allo scorso anno.

Alessandro Marrone, responsabile del programma “Difesa, sicurezza e spazio” dell’Istituto affari internazionali (IAI), ha spiegato a Facta che per comprendere quello che sta accadendo, bisogna «prendere una prospettiva temporale più ampia e una prospettiva settoriale più ampia», così da mettere in connessione episodi che, considerati singolarmente, rischiano di dire poco. Il punto di svolta, nella sua analisi, è l’invasione russa dell’Ucraina nel 2022. Da allora, mentre i Paesi europei hanno intensificato il sostegno militare, economico e politico a Kiev, la Russia ha rafforzato la propria campagna di guerra ibrida contro l’Europa, con un’intensità e una frequenza maggiori rispetto agli anni precedenti. Una campagna che si sarebbe manifestata in modi diversi: dai droni non autorizzati avvistati nei pressi degli aeroporti europei alle navi coinvolte nel danneggiamento di infrastrutture sottomarine, fino ai più recenti allarmi bomba che hanno provocato la sospensione o la deviazione di numerosi voli.

Accanto a una lettura geopolitica, c’è poi quella più tecnica, che permette di capire cosa succede prima che un attacco produca i suoi effetti. «Operazioni di questo tipo non nascono nel momento in cui se ne vedono gli effetti; sono di solito il risultato di un percorso che inizia prima», ha chiarito a Facta Francesca Bosco, vicedirettrice del programma Sicurezza e Tecnologia dell’Istituto delle Nazioni Unite per la ricerca sul disarmo (UNIDIR), un’istituzione autonoma nell’ambito delle Nazioni Unite che svolge ricerche indipendenti su disarmo, controllo degli armamenti e sicurezza internazionale.

Il problema, ha osservato ancora Bosco, è che le «vulnerabilità di questa famiglia di controllori erano state rese pubbliche e corrette dal produttore prima degli episodi», ma migliaia di dispositivi risultavano comunque raggiungibili attraverso Internet. La connessione risponde a esigenze legittime come controllare, ad esempio, che i surgelati siano conservati alla temperatura corretta, ma «le criticità nascono quando la gestione remota si traduce in esposizione diretta, credenziali deboli o apparati che restano in servizio oltre il periodo di supporto». A questo si aggiunge il fatto che «quando molti siti usano gli stessi dispositivi, uno stesso metodo può essere applicato in più luoghi contemporaneamente».

Resta infine la questione della tempistica. Quando una vulnerabilità è nota da tempo, a cambiare non è necessariamente la possibilità tecnica di sfruttarla, ma la volontà di farlo. «Le ragioni della tempistica rimandano a valutazioni di contesto e di intelligence che non sono pubbliche, e non sarebbe corretto speculare», ha precisato Bosco. Al di là dell’identità degli autori, ha concluso, gli episodi che producono conseguenze materiali su servizi essenziali richiedono un’attenzione diversa rispetto a disservizi temporanei, come l’indisponibilità di alcuni siti web.

Quello che è cambiato negli anni, secondo Bosco, è la capacità di chi realizza attacchi ibridi, che oggi sembra riuscire non solo a entrare nei sistemi, ma anche a comprenderne il funzionamento e a intervenire sui processi fisici che controllano. «Anche i falsi allarmi su larga scala sono un fenomeno già osservato in passato», ha aggiunto, ma la novità riguarda soprattutto i settori coinvolti. «Tecnologie operative di uso comune, come la refrigerazione commerciale, finora poco considerate nella definizione delle infrastrutture critiche, entrano nel campo della sicurezza», apportando un cambiamento concettuale, dove non basta più proteggere le infrastrutture tradizionalmente considerate critiche, ma bisogna prestare attenzione anche ai dispositivi collegati a Internet che regolano attività e processi concreti.

“Guerra ibrida”, un termine da usare con precisione

Per comprendere gli episodi recenti è necessario inquadrarli nel contesto più ampio in cui si inseriscono. Sui media e sui social network si è parlato molto di “guerra ibrida” e “cyberattacchi”, termini spesso utilizzati in modo generico, non sempre con piena consapevolezza del loro significato e delle dinamiche che descrivono.

Secondo la definizione adottata dall’Unione europea, le minacce ibride comprendono una combinazione di attività e strumenti convenzionali e non convenzionali – diplomatici, militari, economici e tecnologici – utilizzati in modo coordinato da attori statali o non statali per raggiungere determinati obiettivi, rimanendo al di sotto della soglia di una guerra formalmente dichiarata. Come ha spiegato Francesca Bosco, però, «non esiste una definizione giuridica universalmente condivisa», anche se «le definizioni operative delle istituzioni europee sono convergenti». Il Centro europeo di eccellenza per la lotta alle minacce ibride (Hybrid CoE) di Helsinki, cioè un’organizzazione internazionale autonoma dedicata alla lotta contro le minacce ibride, aggiunge un elemento importante: queste attività sono spesso condotte in modo da non essere immediatamente riconosciute come attacchi e da rendere difficile individuare i responsabili. La guerra ibrida in senso stretto rappresenta invece la fase più acuta di questa strategia.

Secondo Alessandro Marrone l’elemento principale della guerra ibrida sta nel fatto che «esiste un ampio ventaglio di modalità» utilizzate con l’obiettivo politico di «indebolire il sistema Stato, la società civile, il sistema politico, di erodere il consenso verso i partiti mainstream, polarizzare le opinioni e inquinare il dibattito pubblico». Questa ibridazione, per Marrone, permette di rimanere sotto la soglia di attribuzione poiché «non ci sono equipaggiamenti militari chiaramente riconoscibili, come potrebbe essere un battaglione di carri armati» e questo permette di «rimanere sotto la soglia del conflitto convenzionale».

Si tratta di attività difficili da rilevare o da ricondurre a un autore preciso e questo ne rende più difficile la risposta, come ha spiegato Francesca Bosco. Inoltre, attacchi ibridi portano con sé una forte sproporzione dei costi. Una segnalazione, infatti, «richiede pochi minuti a chi la invia può comportare verifiche, evacuazioni e impiego di risorse pubbliche» e in questa logica l’obiettivo può essere non tanto il danno materiale quanto la fiducia dei cittadini nella capacità di risposta delle istituzioni.

Russia, Iran… chi c’è davvero dietro agli attacchi o alle minacce?

Dopo che una serie di allarmi bomba ha bloccato diversi voli e portato all’evacuazione di migliaia di scuole, e dopo la manomissione dei sistemi di refrigerazione di alcuni supermercati, una parte della politica e gran parte del dibattito pubblico si sono concentrati su analisi più o meno affidabili e precise rispetto all’identità degli autori.

Il governo francese ha condannato «con la massima fermezza» la Repubblica islamica dell’Iran attribuendole la responsabilità dell’aumento della temperatura dei frigoriferi e dei congelatori in alcuni supermercati del Paese. Condanne che l’Iran ha respinto, descrivendo le accuse francesi come «infondate e ostili».

In un’intervista rilasciata al Corriere della Sera, Guido Crosetto, ministro italiano della Difesa, ha fatto un riferimento più generale alle ingerenze di Russia, Cina e Iran, sottolineando come queste influenze siano ormai una presenza costante.

Alcuni media italiani hanno parlato di «guerra ibrida dei russi», mentre altri hanno pubblicato lunghe analisi per provare ad analizzare il testo dell’e-mail arrivata alle scuole e firmata “Mikhail Andropov”, cercando di capire chi potesse effettivamente essere il mittente, nonostante fino al momento in cui scriviamo cioè il 18 novembre 2026, nessuna autorità oltre alla Francia abbia effettivamente puntato il dito contro un soggetto specifico o abbia effettivamente collegato tutti gli episodi tra loro.

«Ci vuole molta cautela» ha chiarito Marrone, aggiungendo che esistono autorità preposte alle quali spetta in primo luogo il compito di accertare quanto accaduto e valutare le eventuali responsabilità in caso di attacco. Risalire ai responsabili, infatti, non è facile, anche perché secondo Francesca Bosco «le definizioni europee includono espressamente attori statali e non statali, e la ricerca specializzata descrive un panorama articolato» e chi prepara un accesso non è necessariamente chi lo utilizza. Decisione, coordinamento ed esecuzione possono essere separati, e questa separazione rende più difficile dimostrare il legame tra chi decide e chi esegue.

Bosco ha spiegato anche che nell’ambito delle Nazioni Unite gli Stati si sono impegnati a non ricorrere a soggetti terzi per compiere azioni illegali e a impedire che il proprio territorio venga utilizzato consapevolmente per questo scopo. Per attribuire a uno Stato la responsabilità delle azioni di soggetti privati, però, è necessario dimostrare che abbia dato istruzioni, esercitato una direzione o un controllo sulle loro attività. La semplice tolleranza o un sostegno generico non bastano. Anche quando non è possibile dimostrare un coinvolgimento diretto, uno Stato ha comunque il dovere di intervenire se è a conoscenza di attività illegali svolte sul proprio territorio.

Secondo fonti dei servizi segreti citate dal Financial Times, è attualmente in corso un’indagine coordinata tra vari Stati e condotta dalle agenzie europee di intelligence e sicurezza per risalire all’origine delle minacce che hanno avuto conseguenze sui voli.

Sul fronte della risposta, l’Italia e gli altri Paesi europei stanno cercando di rafforzare gli strumenti di prevenzione e di contrasto. Come ha spiegato Alessandro Marrone, già quasi un anno fa il ministro della Difesa aveva adottato un documento dedicato alla guerra ibrida, con l’obiettivo di sensibilizzare le istituzioni sul livello di rischio e individuare le attività ostili già in corso. Accanto alla ricerca dei responsabili dei singoli episodi, ha aggiunto, c’è anche la volontà di mandare un messaggio chiaro agli eventuali autori di queste operazioni, «la guardia è alta» e le istituzioni stanno monitorando quanto accade.

Ma la risposta non può limitarsi all’individuazione dei responsabili. Secondo Francesca Bosco, gli episodi recenti mostrano soprattutto la necessità di intervenire sulle vulnerabilità dei sistemi: ridurre l’esposizione dei dispositivi industriali a Internet, garantire aggiornamenti e controlli nel tempo, monitorare gli impianti e coinvolgere anche le aziende che si occupano della loro manutenzione. Altrettanto importante è migliorare la capacità di riconoscere tempestivamente le anomalie e conservare le prove utili alle indagini. Sul fronte degli allarmi, invece, serve una gestione proporzionata delle segnalazioni, capace di distinguere i messaggi seriali da quelli accompagnati da elementi concreti di pericolo.

La sfida, dunque, non riguarda soltanto la capacità di reagire a un attacco, ma soprattutto quella di prepararsi, ridurre le vulnerabilità e rendere più resilienti istituzioni, imprese e servizi essenziali. Perché, come mostrano gli episodi delle ultime settimane, anche attività che non provocano danni materiali possono mettere sotto pressione le istituzioni e incidere sulla fiducia dei cittadini nella loro capacità di garantire la sicurezza.

articles.title: Il ceo di Anthropic Amodei in Puglia per seguire la ristrutturazione della sua masseria
articles.summary: L'immobile vicino Borgo Egnazia. Non è escluso che abbia individuato altri resort
articles.preview: Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, in Puglia da venerdì, starebbe seguendo i lavori di ristrutturazione di Masseria Minerva, acquistata nell'agosto del 2024, dopo il G7 che si è tenuto a Borgo Egnazia a giugno dello stesso anno. Masseria Minerva si trova a pochi chilometri da Borgo Egnazia, precisamente a Pozzo Faceto, frazione di Fasano, in provincia di Brindisi. L'acquisto di una masseria (riportato da Repubblica Bari), sarebbe un primo investimento, in questo caso per realizzare una residenza privata per la coppia.
articles.body:
Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, in Puglia da venerdì, starebbe seguendo i lavori di ristrutturazione di Masseria Minerva, acquistata nell'agosto del 2024, dopo il G7 che si è tenuto a Borgo Egnazia a giugno dello stesso anno. Masseria Minerva si trova a pochi chilometri da Borgo Egnazia, precisamente a Pozzo Faceto, frazione di Fasano, in provincia di Brindisi.

L'acquisto di una masseria (riportato da Repubblica Bari), sarebbe un primo investimento, in questo caso per realizzare una residenza privata per la coppia. E non è escluso, come viene riferito da più fonti, che Amodei possa aver già individuato altre masserie o resort da acquistare.

Gli adempimenti burocratici per l'acquisto e i primi lavori di Masseria Minerva, sono stati seguiti da sua moglie Cami Clark e da un team specializzato che collabora con il manager italo-americano. Cami Clark in questi mesi avrebbe avuto contatti diretti anche con amministratori del Comune di Fasano.

Amodei in questi giorni starebbe soggiornando a Borgo Egnazia dove c'è anche un evento organizzato da Reply, una società italiana di consulenza e servizi informatici. L'azienda, a quanto si apprende, si occupa, tra l'altro, di intelligenza artificiale e analisi dei dati, cloud e infrastrutture digitali, e cybersecurity.

articles.title: A tale of two Nvidias
articles.summary: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia — the company’s latest earnings report vs. the tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang’s return.
articles.preview: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
articles.body:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Kirsten: Sure, never say never.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.

Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

articles.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
articles.summary: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.
articles.preview: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry.
